It solves stress and strain over a mesh and suits smooth, large tools, but large deformations need remeshing or arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian (ALE) methods. Discrete element method (DEM) treats soil as many particles with contact laws. It captures flow, mixing and fragmentation, but is computationally expensive and its parameters are not direct soil properties. Coupled FEM-DEM models are used for mixed problems.

sections.heading: Calibration and validation
sections.text: Calibration adjusts model parameters until predictions match measured data, for example draught, penetration resistance or soil disturbance in a soil bin. Validation then tests the calibrated model against independent field measurements at different moisture contents and speeds. Report both, and state boundary conditions and scale effects.

keyPoints: Soil strength is described by the Mohr-Coulomb criterion, τ = c′ + σ′ tan φ′.
Constitutive models such as Mohr-Coulomb, Drucker-Prager and Cam-clay link stress to strain; parameters must be measured, not assumed.
Draught rises with depth, width, speed and soil strength; traction depends on slip and is net of motion resistance.
FEM suits continuum stress analysis but needs remeshing for large deformation; DEM suits granular flow but is costly and needs calibration.
Calibrate models against soil-bin or field data, then validate against independent field measurements.
Report boundary conditions, moisture content and scale effects, because soil behaviour is highly variable.

en.title: Advanced crop water and irrigation modelling
en.short: Modelling evapotranspiration, soil water, crop growth, remote sensing and irrigation optimisation.

sections.heading: ET and balance
sections.text:
Evapotranspiration (ET) is water lost as vapour from soil and plants. Reference evapotranspiration ET0 is the demand of a well-watered reference crop, often estimated with the FAO Penman-Monteith equation. The crop coefficient Kc scales ET0 to potential crop ET. A stress coefficient Ks reduces it when soil water is limiting, so actual ET is ETa = Ks × Kc × ET0.

The root-zone water balance is ΔS = P + I + U − ETa − D − R, where S is stored water, P precipitation, I irrigation, U upward flux, D drainage and R runoff, all in mm.

Example: ET0 = 5 mm/day, Kc = 0.8, Ks = 0.75, so ETa = 3 mm/day. With P = 10 mm, I = 20 mm, U = D = 0 and R = 5 mm, ΔS = 10 + 20 − 3 − 5 = 22 mm.

sections.heading: Crop models
sections.text: Crop growth simulation models represent processes such as phenology, canopy expansion, biomass accumulation and yield over time, driven by weather, soil water and management. Examples include DSSAT, APSIM and AquaCrop. Calibration adjusts cultivar and soil parameters so simulated values match measured data. Validation then tests the model on independent data, using measures such as root mean square error (RMSE) and bias. Report both calibration and validation; a model fitted to one season may fail in another.

sections.heading: Remote sensing and optimisation
sections.text: Remote sensing estimates actual ET over fields from satellite land surface temperature and vegetation indices, often through surface energy balance models. Deficit irrigation deliberately applies less water than full ET, accepting some yield loss to save water or raise water productivity. Optimisation chooses water allocation or schedules to maximise yield, net return or water productivity under constraints. Climate scenario analysis uses global and regional climate model projections, with downscaling and bias correction, to test irrigation plans. Projections carry uncertainty, so use ensembles and report ranges. Design standards and registration rules differ by country; check the current national code.

keyPoints: Actual ET is ETa = Ks × Kc × ET0, where Ks is the water stress coefficient.
Root-zone soil water balance: ΔS = P + I + U − ETa − D − R.
Calibrate crop models on measured data and validate on independent data, reporting RMSE and bias.
Remote sensing estimates ET from land surface temperature and vegetation indices.
Deficit irrigation accepts some yield loss to save water or raise water productivity.
Climate scenario results are uncertain, so use ensembles, report ranges and check national design rules.

en.title: Advanced food process and drying modelling
en.short: Drying kinetics, coupled heat and mass transfer, glass transition, quality kinetics and process simulation.

sections.heading: Drying kinetics
sections.text:
Drying removes water by evaporation. The moisture ratio is MR = (M − Me) ÷ (M0 − Me), where M is dry-basis moisture, M0 initial and Me equilibrium. Thin-layer models describe a thin sample dried under constant drying conditions. Lewis: MR = exp(−kt). Page: MR = exp(−kt^n), with k a rate constant and n a dimensionless exponent. They are empirical: fit them to data for each material and dryer.

Example: M0 = 5.0, Me = 0.10, M = 1.0 kg water/kg dry matter at t = 2 h.
MR = (1.0 − 0.10) ÷ (5.0 − 0.10) = 0.184
Page with n = 1.2: ln MR = −1.693 = −k(2^1.2); 2^1.2 = 2.297, so k = 0.737 h^−1.2. Check: exp(−0.737 × 2.297) = 0.184.

sections.heading: Coupled transfer
sections.text: Heat and mass transfer are coupled. Evaporation cools the surface, so heat flows from the air, while water moves inside by diffusion, capillarity and pressure gradients. A coupled model solves moisture and energy balances with convective boundary conditions. The Biot number compares internal and surface resistance. For a slab, the leading diffusion term is MR ≈ (8 ÷ π²) exp(−π² Deff t ÷ (4L²)), where Deff is the effective diffusivity and L is half-thickness. Use it only when diffusion controls.

sections.heading: Glass transition and quality
sections.text: Glass transition temperature Tg marks the change from a rigid glassy state to a rubbery state. In a state diagram, Tg falls as water content rises. Above Tg, stickiness, caking and collapse are likely. Quality kinetics describe loss of colour, vitamins or texture. Many follow first order: C = C0 exp(−kt), with k = A exp(−Ea ÷ RT) from the Arrhenius equation. Validate predictions for the food.

sections.heading: Non-thermal and simulation
sections.text: Non-thermal processes include high hydrostatic pressure, pulsed electric fields, ultrasound, cold plasma and irradiation. Effectiveness and legal approval differ by country, so check the current national regulator. Simulation uses mass and energy balances, often solved by finite differences. Optimisation chooses variables such as air temperature and flow rate to minimise energy or quality loss under constraints. Validate models against measured data.

keyPoints: Moisture ratio: MR = (M − Me) ÷ (M0 − Me).
Lewis model: MR = exp(−kt); Page model: MR = exp(−kt^n).
Coupled drying models solve heat and mass balances together; the Biot number compares internal and surface resistance.
Glass transition temperature Tg falls as water content rises; above Tg, stickiness and collapse are likely.
First-order quality loss: C = C0 exp(−kt), with k = A exp(−Ea ÷ RT).
Non-thermal process approval varies by country; simulation and optimisation must be validated against measured data.

en.title: Research methods and the dissertation
en.short: Forming a problem, reviewing literature, designing experiments, analysing data, modelling and dissertation defence.

sections.heading: From problem to question
sections.text:
A research problem is a gap in knowledge or a practical failure that a study can address. Turn it into answerable objectives and hypotheses. A hypothesis is a testable statement; an objective is what you will do. A good problem is narrow enough to finish within your time and resources.

Read the literature systematically: find what is known, what conflicts and what methods others used. Keep a reference manager. Cite every borrowed idea. Referencing styles such as APA, Harvard and Vancouver differ; follow your department’s guide. Plagiarism is presenting another person’s words, data or ideas as your own, even without intent.

sections.heading: Design and measurement
sections.text:
Experimental design controls nuisance variation so treatment effects are visible. Define experimental units, treatments, replicates and randomisation. Blocking groups similar experimental units to reduce known sources of variation. A factorial design tests two or more factors together. Instrumentation must be calibrated; record calibration dates and uncertainties.

Example: a drying trial with temperature (40, 50 °C) and air speed (1, 2 m/s) in three replicates has 2 × 2 × 3 = 12 runs. Randomise run order to avoid drift. Data analysis follows the design: check assumptions, then use ANOVA or regression. Report means with a measure of uncertainty.

sections.heading: Models, ethics and defence
sections.text:
A model is a simplified representation; validation checks it against independent data. For predicted and measured values 0.60/0.62, 0.45/0.43, 0.30/0.33, differences are −0.02, 0.02, −0.03; squares sum to 0.0017; RMSE = √(0.0017 ÷ 3) = 0.024. Ethics covers honest data, consent, animal welfare, safety and permits. Professional registration differs by country; in Nigeria, COREN registers engineers.

Write the dissertation as a clear argument: problem, method, results, discussion, conclusion. Keep raw data and analysis scripts for audit. In the viva, defend choices, acknowledge limits and answer precisely.

keyPoints: A research problem must be answerable, with clear objectives and testable hypotheses.
The literature review shows the gap; cite every source and follow your department’s referencing style.
Randomise, replicate and block to control nuisance variation; calibrate instruments and record uncertainty.
Analyse data according to the design, checking assumptions before ANOVA or regression.
Validate models on independent data; RMSE = √(Σ(predicted − measured)² ÷ n).
Plagiarism is presenting others’ work as your own; keep raw data, follow ethics rules and defend your limits in the viva.
